analysis.investment_thesis: Cigniti is a fundamentally sound, nearly debt-free software testing specialist with 26% ROE and a cheap 11.7x P/E — but as a subsidiary of Coforge (post-Dec 2024 acquisition), minority shareholders face delisting risk and loss of independent strategic control. The business quality is real, but the corporate structure overhang limits conviction for a long-term bet.
key_strengths: Exceptional capital efficiency: ROE 26%, ROCE 34%, D/E near zero (0.02) with INR 199 Cr cash vs. INR 28 Cr debt
Consistent free cash generation: FCF positive all 5 years, INR 147 Cr FCF in FY25 on near-zero capex — asset-light model
Revenue accelerating: 14.5% 9-year CAGR with clear inflection post-FY21 (INR 897 Cr → INR 2,014 Cr by FY25)
key_risks: Coforge subsidiary status is the #1 risk — potential forced delisting at a price set by the acquirer, leaving minority shareholders with little recourse
US-revenue concentration: QA/testing exports are highly sensitive to US tech capex cycles and visa/offshoring policy shifts
Narrow moat in commoditized testing services — IP-led tools help, but pricing power is limited vs. larger Tier-1 IT peers
red_flags: Coforge now controls 54%+ — independent management vision gone; minority shareholders are passengers, not partners
FY17 catastrophic loss of INR 395 Cr (other income line shows -332 Cr) signals a historical impairment/write-off of serious magnitude — management quality pre-2020 was questionable
Not an India domestic consumption story — revenue is predominantly US/international IT services, limiting alignment with India's structural GDP tailwinds I typically seek
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Cigniti's numbers are genuinely attractive on the surface: P/E of 11.7x for a company compounding revenues at 14.5% and profits at 16.7% over 9 years, with ROCE of 34% and virtually no debt, is a setup I would normally get excited about. The operating margin has expanded to 17% in FY25, FCF is healthy at INR 147 Cr, and the balance sheet has been dramatically cleaned up — borrowings fell from INR 121 Cr in FY20 to just INR 20 Cr in FY25 while cash ballooned to INR 199 Cr. The business model (software testing and quality engineering) is asset-light, recurring, and benefits from growing software complexity globally.

However, the December 2024 Coforge acquisition fundamentally changes the investment calculus for a minority shareholder. In India, when a promoter crosses 75%, SEBI's delisting regulations become the governing framework — and acquirers routinely delist subsidiaries at values that don't reflect full fair value. I cannot take a large conviction position in a company where the controlling shareholder can effectively set the exit price. Additionally, this is an IT export story, not an India consumption or infrastructure play — the structural tailwinds I seek (rising domestic incomes, financial inclusion, urbanization) are not the growth drivers here. At current prices, this is fairly valued for a trapped minority holder, not a compounding opportunity.
